Its candidate hash matches the frozen provenance and its decoded proof hash matches the intake source digest. Sections 1–4 and equations (1)–(8) give the same ordinary-uniform deformation and weighted objective. The frozen result allows C² bumps, makes the compact-support shell margin explicit, and supplies the radial differentiability argument. The source imposes section-centroid and coarea hypotheses for its application, which the deformation and cap algebra do not need. The separate deepest-point argument and disk calibration in sections 5–6 are outside the reviewed claim.

On the compact closure of a sufficiently small neighborhood of the bump support, the least eigenvalue of A_h has a positive lower bound and A_psi is bounded. The homogeneous extension has tangential Hessian A_(h+t psi)/r and zero radial and mixed blocks there. Outside the support it locally equals the original convex extension even at singular normals. These neighborhoods cover all nonzero points, so each line avoiding zero has a convex restriction. On a line through zero the two slopes are -h_t(-n) and h_t(n), in increasing order by positivity. Global convexity follows on all lines. The dominated linear forms represent this finite homogeneous convex function, and the positive minimum and finite maximum of h_t give an inner ball and an outer bound. The support norm bound gives Hausdorff convergence.

Differentiability on the smooth patch gives the unique support point h_t n + grad_S h_t. Outside the closed support the two convex extensions have the same local subdifferential and hence the same full support face. If a radial endpoint differs, a supporting normal outside the support at either endpoint would place that endpoint on both boundaries, contrary to uniqueness along the ray. Compactness gives a strictly positive common signed cutting-form margin for both endpoints for all sufficiently small signed t. Each signed cutting form is linear along the connecting segment, so the same margin applies to every point of every changed interval. The cutting forms use unit normals, making this also a uniform distance bound.

For s_i=1 the entire changed shell lies in H_i and for s_i=-1 it lies outside H_i. Integrating the signed difference of indicators gives exactly e_i times the signed volume change in both cases, and summing gives the new numerator V Phi(K) + W Delta V. Subtracting Phi(K) after dividing by V_t yields the displayed quotient. Inclusion is strict in the indicated direction since a nonzero nonnegative psi changes the support function somewhere, and any strict inclusion of these full-dimensional convex bodies leaves a positive-volume difference.

On the smooth neighborhood the derivative of X_t has image n-perp and equals A_(h_t). A second normal at X_t(n) would supply intervening normals arbitrarily close to n with the same support point. The two normals cannot be antipodal because the origin is interior. This contradicts local injectivity. Radial projection of n-perp onto X_t(n)-perp is nonsingular since n dot X_t(n)=h_t(n)>0. Applying the inverse function theorem to (t,n) and taking a finite cover of the compact image of the bump support at t=0 gives uniform small t and fixed local inverse patches. The radial endpoints agree on overlaps, and every direction that can change is covered because the old endpoint has a support normal in the bump support. Taking a scalar product with n_t gives partial_t rho=psi(n_t)/(n_t dot omega). The denominator is uniformly positive by the inner and outer ball bounds. Differentiation under the sphere integral gives a continuous volume derivative. The radial Jacobian is (n dot omega)/rho^(d-1), which converts that integral at t=0 to the stated surface integral. Normals with psi>0 yield a nonempty open boundary patch of positive area by the full-rank parametrization, so the derivative is strictly positive.

Since both signs of t give arbitrarily small Hausdorff changes with the same sections, W below Phi gives descent for t>0 and W above Phi gives descent for t<0. Section area, first moment and coarea balance with fixed normals and weights are preserved by exact set equality. In an unoriented plane class the two cap volumes add to V because their common boundary is null for d-dimensional volume. If both orientation weights equal a, that class contributes a to Phi and weight 2a, so balance across all classes gives exactly 1/2. A single-plane crossing changes W by the difference of the two orientation weights up to the direction of crossing. In the globally positive-curvature case, a nonzero ray on the chosen plane avoids all other distinct planes by the finite proper subspace argument, including in d=2. Its radial endpoint cannot have normal parallel to the cutting normal, because a supporting plane through 0 would violate interiority. Full rank of DX gives transversality and open normal patches on both sides. The same argument applies at an isolated crossing in a locally smooth patch.

overlap.comparison: Proves continuity of proper section areas under Hausdorff and plane perturbations. It does not construct a perturbation that fixes sections as sets or determine finite signed cap changes.

Identifies centroid contacts and coarea circuits under regularity assumptions for mixed depth regions. The present lemma preserves section centroids if given, using an ordinary uniform-body path that the contact theorem does not provide.

Uses a sign fan to vary source triangles and weights in a planar three-fan, with an estimate on a maximum score. This gives neither a local support perturbation of a general body nor exact central section traces and weighted-cap identities.

Gives the ordinary maximal-depth minimum and its simplex rigidity, and uses a change of center on a fixed body. Its functional and admissible variations differ from those of the fixed-section weighted menu.
